'''Panama''' is a cryptographic primitive which can be used both as a [[hash function]] and a [[stream cipher]], but its hash function mode of operation has been broken and is not suitable for cryptographic use.  Based on [[StepRightUp]], it was designed by [[Joan Daemen]] and Craig Clapp and presented in the paper ''Fast Hashing and Stream Encryption with PANAMA'' on the Fast Software Encryption (FSE) conference 1998.<ref>{{Cite conference |title=Fast Hashing and Stream Encryption with PANAMA |conference=FSE '98: Proceedings of the 5th International Workshop on Fast Software Encryption |last=Daemen |first=Joan |author-link=Joan Daemen |last2=Clapp |first2=Craig S. K. |year=1998 |doi=10.1007/3-540-69710-1_5 |isbn=354064265X |doi-access=free}}</ref>  The cipher has influenced several other designs, for example [[MUGI]] and [[SHA-3]].<ref name="FixingPanama">https://csrc.nist.gov/groups/ST/hash/sha-3/documents/Keccak-slides-at-NIST.pdf On slide 5, it states the "starting
point: fixing Panama"</ref><ref>{{cite journal
|url=https://drops.dagstuhl.de/opus/volltexte/2009/1958/
|title=The Road from Panama to Keccak via RadioGatún
|author1=Bertoni, Guido |author2=Daemen, Joan |author3=Peeters, Michaël |author4=Van Assche, Gilles |journal=Drops-Idn/V2/Document/10.4230/Dagsemproc.09031.17
|series=Dagstuhl Seminar Proceedings (DagSemProc)
|year=2009
|volume=9031
|pages=1–9
|doi=10.4230/DagSemProc.09031.17
|doi-access=free
|access-date=2009-10-20
}}</ref>

The primitive can be used both as a [[hash function]] and a [[stream cipher]]. The stream cipher uses a 256-bit key and the performance of the cipher is very good reaching 2 [[cycles per byte]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Panama Cryptographic Function |url=https://www.drdobbs.com/security/the-panama-cryptographic-function/184410745 |last=Daemen |first=Joan |date=1998-12-01 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240904184824/https://www.drdobbs.com/security/the-panama-cryptographic-function/184410745 |archive-date=2024-09-04 |access-date=2026-01-14 |website=[[Dr. Dobb's Journal]] |author-link=Joan Daemen |last2=Clapp |first2=Craig}}</ref>

==Hash function==
{{Infobox encryption method
|name           = Panama (hash)
|digest size    = 256 bits
|related to     = 
|certification  = 
|key size       = 
|security claim = 2<sup>128</sup> (collision resistance)
|state size     = 8736 bits
|block size     = 256 bits
|cryptanalysis  = Panama hash collisions can be generated in 2<sup>6</sup> time.<ref name=fse2007 />
}}
As a hash function, collisions have been shown by [[Vincent Rijmen]] et al. in the paper ''Producing Collisions for PANAMA'' presented at FSE 2001. The attack shows a [[Computational complexity theory|computational complexity]] of 2<sup>82</sup> and with negligible memory requirements.<ref>{{cite conference |author=Vincent Rijmen |author2=Bart Van Rompay |author3=Bart Preneel |author4=Joos Vandewalle |year=2001 |title=Producing Collisions for PANAMA |conference=FSE 2001 |url=https://www.cosic.esat.kuleuven.be/publications/article-81.ps }}</ref>

At FSE 2007, Joan Daemen and Gilles Van Assche presented a practical attack on the Panama hash function that generates a collision in 2<sup>6</sup> evaluations of the state updating function.<ref name=fse2007>{{cite conference |author=Joan Daemen |author2=Gilles Van Assche |date=2007-04-04 |title=Producing Collisions for Panama, Instantaneously |conference=FSE 2007 |url=https://radiogatun.noekeon.org/panama/ }}</ref>

Guido Bertoni, [[Joan Daemen]], Michaël Peeters, and Gilles Van Assche, at [[NIST]]'s 2006 Second Cryptographic Hash Workshop, unveiled a Panama variant called [[RadioGatún]]. The hash function workings of RadioGatún does not have the known weaknesses that Panama's hash function has.  In turn, RadioGatún inspired the new cryptographic standard [[SHA-3]].<ref name="FixingPanama" />
